title: Given two strings, find the minimum number of deletions and insertions needed to transform the first string into the second, using only deletions and insertions. Explain how the Longest Common Substring pattern solves it through the longest common subsequence, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Minimum Deletions and Insertions to Transform One String into Another

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Deletions and Insertions to Transform One String into Another is solved with the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence. The shared subsequence is kept, every character of the first string outside it is deleted, and every character of the second string outside it is inserted. So deletions equal the first length minus the common subsequence, and insertions equal the second length minus the common subsequence. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India migrates an old account label into a new standard label and wants to know the fewest removals and additions to convert one into the other. Whatever the two labels share in order is kept, the rest of the old label is deleted, and the missing parts of the new label are inserted.

**One line to remember:** Deletions equal first length minus common subsequence, insertions equal second length minus common subsequence.

sections.s2_technical:
The key realisation is that any character belonging to the longest common subsequence can stay in place during the transformation, because it appears in both strings in the same relative order. Every character of the first string that is not part of that shared subsequence must be deleted, and every character of the second string that is not part of it must be inserted. So the number of deletions is the length of the first string minus the common subsequence length, and the number of insertions is the length of the second string minus the common subsequence length.

We compute the longest common subsequence with the standard prefix table: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);` then deletions are `m - dp[m][n]` and insertions are `n - dp[m][n]`. A concrete check: turning a six-character label into a five-character label with a four-character shared subsequence needs two deletions and one insertion. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, it uses only deletions and insertions so it is simpler than full edit distance that also allows substitution, and both answers come from the single common subsequence value.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is migrating old account labels into a new standard labelling scheme and needs, for each label, the fewest removals and additions to convert the old label into the new one using only deletions and insertions. Trying all edit sequences is exponential. This is exactly how Minimum Deletions and Insertions works: it computes the longest common subsequence with the Longest Common Substring pattern and derives both counts from it.

The code defines a `LabelMigrationService` exposing `transformCost(oldLabel, newLabel)` returning a small result with the deletions and insertions. A `Demo` runs it over two sample labels and logs both counts.

sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are the old label SAVINGS and the new label SAVING. We want the fewest deletions and insertions to convert the first into the second.

Step 1 — We build the longest common subsequence table aligning SAVINGS down the rows and SAVING across the columns.

Step 2 — The characters S, A, V, I, N, G all match in order, so the shared subsequence grows to six as each matching character extends the diagonal.

Step 3 — The final S in SAVINGS has no partner left in SAVING, so it does not extend the shared subsequence, and the corner value stays at six.

Step 4 — Deletions equal the old length seven minus six, which is one, namely the trailing S. Insertions equal the new length six minus six, which is zero.

Step 5 — The service returns one deletion and zero insertions, which matches dropping the trailing S to turn SAVINGS into SAVING. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:25:19 PM com.bank.labelmig.service.LabelMigrationService transformCost
INFO: Transform SAVINGS to SAVING: deletions=1 insertions=0
Oct 27, 2026 9:25:19 PM com.bank.labelmig.LabelMigrationApplication main
INFO: Deletions 1, insertions 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: old = "SAVINGS" (7), new = "SAVING" (6)
    │
    ▼
  longest common subsequence table
    │ S,A,V,I,N,G match in order → LCS = 6
    │ trailing S unmatched
    ▼
  deletions = 7 - 6 = 1   insertions = 6 - 6 = 0
    ▼
  Output: delete 1 (trailing S), insert 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Deletions and Insertions to Transform One String into Another is a neat application of the Longest Common Substring pattern through its subsequence form. The insight is that any character belonging to the longest common subsequence of the two strings can remain untouched during the transformation, because it already appears in both strings in the same relative order. Everything else in the first string has to be deleted, and everything missing from the second string has to be inserted.

So I compute the longest common subsequence once with the standard prefix table, and then the number of deletions is the first string's length minus that shared length, while the number of insertions is the second string's length minus the same shared length. Both answers fall out of a single quadratic time and space computation. I usually point out that because this problem allows only deletions and insertions, not substitutions, it is simpler than the full edit distance and maps directly onto the common subsequence.

At the National Bank of India I used this while migrating old account labels into a new standard scheme, where the team needed the fewest removals and additions to convert each old label into its new form. I computed the longest common subsequence and derived both counts from it. Explaining that the shared subsequence stays, the extra old characters are deleted, the missing new characters are inserted, and that both numbers come from one common subsequence value is what shows an interviewer I understand this use of the Longest Common Substring pattern.
